content: Asparagus officinalis is a plant species belonging to the family Asparagaceae, from which the well-known vegetable asparagus is derived. This species likely originated in the eastern Mediterranean region but is now cultivated widely as a vegetable crop. Biology Asparagus officinalis is native to maritime areas surrounding the Mediterranean. While traditionally classified within the Liliaceae family, some taxonomists have separated it into the Asparagaceae family. Only the young shoots of asparagus are consumed, as they are harvested before they grow into feathery structures that can reach heights of 100–150 cm. The leaves of the plant are actually needle-like cladodes, which are modified stems located in the axils of scale leaves. Male and female flowers typically grow on separate plants, although hermaphroditic flowers are occasionally observed. The flowers are found at the junctions of the branchlets, either singly or in groups of two to three. The fruit of the plant is a small red berry. Asparagus is a low-calorie food that contains no fat or cholesterol and has very low sodium levels. It is a good source of folic acid, potassium, fiber, and rutin. The amino acid asparagine, which is abundant in asparagus, derives its name from this plant. History Asparagus has been used since ancient times both as a vegetable and as a medicinal plant, valued for its delicate flavor and diuretic properties. A recipe for cooking asparagus appears in the oldest surviving cookbook, De re coquinaria by Apicius, dating back to the 3rd century AD. Although its popularity waned during the Middle Ages, asparagus regained favor in the 17th century. Uses Culinary Asparagus shoots can be prepared and served in various ways, though they are most commonly boiled or steamed and served with hollandaise sauce, melted butter, or olive oil and Parmesan cheese. Specialized tall asparagus cooking pots allow the shoots to be gently steamed. In Cantonese cuisine, asparagus is often stir-fried with chicken, shrimp, or beef, and it is sometimes wrapped in bacon. Asparagus can also be quickly grilled over charcoal or hardwood embers. The best asparagus is typically the early growth of the season, which is often simply steamed and served with melted butter. Proper preparation is essential, as the bottom portion of the asparagus often contains sand. It is worth noting that a case of botulism linked to asparagus was recorded in Australia in 1991. Medicinal The rhizomes and roots of asparagus are used in ethnomedicine to treat urinary tract infections, as well as kidney and bladder stones. Some compounds in asparagus are metabolized and excreted in the urine, producing a distinctive odor. This odor is caused by sulfur-containing compounds such as thiols and thioesters, as well as ammonia. Recent studies suggest that all individuals produce these odorous compounds after consuming asparagus, but only about 40% of people have the genetic ability to detect the smell. The onset of the odor in urine occurs rapidly, within 15–30 minutes of ingestion. Cultivation Asparagus thrives in soils that are too saline for most weeds, as it originates from maritime habitats. Historically, a small amount of salt was used to suppress weeds in asparagus beds, though this practice rendered the soil unsuitable for other crops. Asparagus crowns are planted in winter, and the first shoots appear in spring. The initial harvests, known as sprue asparagus, have thin stems. White asparagus, or spargel, is cultivated by depriving the plants of light and increasing their exposure to ultraviolet light during growth. This variety is less bitter than green asparagus and is particularly popular in the Netherlands and Germany, where 57,000 tons (61% of consumer demand) are produced annually. Purple asparagus, which has higher sugar and lower fiber content than green or white varieties, was originally developed in Italy under the variety name Violetto d'Albenga. Breeding efforts have since continued in countries such as the United States and New Zealand. Commercial Production Peru is currently the world’s leading exporter of asparagus, followed by China and Mexico. The largest importers of asparagus in 2004 were the United States (92,405 tons), the European Union (18,565 tons), and Japan (17,148 tons). In 2005, the United States produced asparagus on 54,000 acres (220 km²), yielding 90,200 tons, making it the world’s largest producer and consumer. Production was concentrated in California, Michigan, and Washington. In California’s Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta region, asparagus is celebrated annually with a festival in Stockton. In the United Kingdom, the Vale of Evesham is the traditional center of asparagus production, with British asparagus noted for its more delicate flavor compared to varieties grown in hotter climates. Vernacular Names and Etymology Asparagus officinalis is commonly referred to simply as asparagus, though it may be confused with unrelated plant species also called asparagus, such as Ornithogalum pyrenaicum (known as Prussian asparagus for its edible shoots). The English word asparagus derives from classical Latin, but the plant was once known in English as sperage, from the Medieval Latin sparagus. This term originates from the Greek aspharagos or asparagos, which in turn comes from the Persian asparag, meaning sprout or shoot. In some regions, the name was corrupted to sparrow grass. John Walker noted in 1791 that sparrow-grass was so widely used that asparagus seemed overly formal and pedantic. In parts of Texas, the plant is colloquially referred to as aspar grass or asper grass. In fruit retail circles, it is sometimes called Sparrows Guts, a term distinct from the older sparrow grass. In French and Dutch, it is known as asperge, in Portuguese as espargo hortense, and in German as Spargel.
